boc-1-218.explanation: Drug-independent antibodies behave like warm autoantibodies even without drug in the test. They commonly produce IgG-coated cells and broad serum/eluate reactivity.
optionExplanations: IgG-positive DAT plus positive screen matches the pattern.
A negative eluate is less typical of this warm-autoantibody pattern.
Complement-only coating with negative screen suggests another mechanism.
A negative DAT does not fit the usual coated-cell pattern.
boc-1-218.memory: Drug-independent antibodies can mimic warm AIHA.

quickCheck.question: Must drug be present in the test for a drug-independent antibody to react?
quickCheck.answer: No; it reacts without added drug.

boc-1-219.questionInPlainEnglish: Which antibody is classically responsible for PCH?
boc-1-219.explanation: The Donath–Landsteiner antibody is usually IgG anti-P. It binds in cooler conditions and causes complement-mediated hemolysis after warming.
optionExplanations: Cold-reactive IgG anti-P is the classic combination.
IgM is the wrong class for the classic PCH antibody.
I is the wrong target for classic PCH.
IgM anti-I fits cold agglutinin disease instead.

quickCheck.question: Why is PCH called biphasic?
quickCheck.answer: Binding and hemolysis occur at different temperature phases.

boc-1-220.questionInPlainEnglish: Which process destroys red cells inside the blood vessels?
boc-1-220.explanation: Complement activation through the final membrane attack complex ruptures cells in circulation. Macrophage removal of coated cells instead occurs mainly outside vessels.
optionExplanations: Phagocyte destruction is mainly extravascular.
Complete complement activation can cause intravascular lysis.
Phagocyte clearance of complement-coated cells is extravascular.
Stopping at C3b marks cells but does not form the lytic pore.

quickCheck.question: What happens when complement stops at C3b?
quickCheck.answer: Cells may be tagged for macrophage clearance instead of rupturing directly.

boc-1-221.questionInPlainEnglish: Which example most strongly points to red-cell destruction outside the vessels?
boc-1-221.explanation: Delayed Kidd reactions commonly involve macrophage clearance of coated donor cells. This is extravascular destruction, unlike the classic rapid complement lysis of ABO-incompatible red cells.
optionExplanations: A cells into an O recipient risk acute intravascular hemolysis.
A plasma can be compatible with O recipient red cells.
Delayed anti-Jka reactions commonly cause extravascular clearance.
A previously unsensitized person has no existing anti-D for immediate destruction.
boc-1-221.memory: Delayed IgG reactions often use spleen/liver clearance.

quickCheck.question: Does a first D-positive exposure guarantee immediate anti-D hemolysis?
quickCheck.answer: No; existing antibody and later sensitization are different issues.

boc-1-221.sourceNote: D-positive exposure can still cause alloimmunization; this is an educational mechanism comparison.

boc-1-222.questionInPlainEnglish: Which disease setting suits returning a person's own stored blood-forming cells?
boc-1-222.explanation: After high-dose cancer chemotherapy, autologous stem cells can rebuild damaged marrow. They do not replace an inherited defective gene with a healthy donor version.
optionExplanations: Hodgkin lymphoma treatment may use autologous marrow rescue.
The person's own cells retain an inherited hemoglobin defect.
The person's own cells retain a congenital immune defect.
The person's own cells retain an inherited metabolic defect.
boc-1-222.memory: Autologous transplant rescues marrow after intensive therapy.

quickCheck.question: Why use another donor for many inherited blood disorders?
quickCheck.answer: Healthy donor cells can supply a working gene function.

boc-1-223.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement correctly identifies sources of blood-forming stem/progenitor cells?
boc-1-223.explanation: These cells can be collected from marrow, umbilical cord blood, or blood after medications mobilize them out of marrow.
optionExplanations: A fixed five-of-ten minimum is not a universal transplant success rule.
Marrow, cord blood and mobilized blood are recognized sources.
Marrow harvest is not universally preferred or less burdensome.
A mandatory six-hour infusion is not the stated practice.
boc-1-223.memory: Three sources: marrow, cord, mobilized peripheral blood.

quickCheck.question: What does mobilization mean here?
quickCheck.answer: Encouraging blood-forming cells to move from marrow into circulating blood.

boc-1-223.sourceNote: Modern donor options include haploidentical transplantation; the source's matching thresholds are simplified.

boc-1-224.questionInPlainEnglish: What red-cell modification is important immediately after marrow transplantation?
boc-1-224.explanation: Irradiation prevents donor T cells from multiplying in a vulnerable transplant recipient. It addresses graft-versus-host disease risk, not just anemia.
optionExplanations: Packed cells alone do not address donor T-cell risk.
Washing removes plasma but does not adequately disable T cells.
Microaggregate filtration is not a substitute for irradiation.
Irradiated red cells prevent donor T-cell proliferation.
boc-1-224.memory: Transplant support needs irradiated cellular products.

quickCheck.question: Does leukocyte filtration replace required irradiation?
quickCheck.answer: No; residual viable T cells may remain.

boc-1-225.questionInPlainEnglish: Which antigen system connects transplantation and several immune transfusion reactions?
boc-1-225.explanation: HLA markers identify cells to the immune system. HLA matching and antibodies affect transplanted tissue, donor immune cells, platelets, and some lung or fever reactions.
optionExplanations: Rh mainly concerns red-cell compatibility.
HLA connects all the listed immune settings.
Lewis does not explain the transplantation and platelet links.
Diego mainly concerns red-cell antigens.
boc-1-225.memory: HLA is a major immune identity system.

quickCheck.question: Why can HLA antibodies affect both platelets and transplantation?
quickCheck.answer: Both platelets and transplanted cells display HLA markers.

boc-1-226.questionInPlainEnglish: Which markers belong to HLA class II?
boc-1-226.explanation: HLA-DR, DQ and DP help present material to helper T cells. They occur mainly on specialized antigen-presenting cells rather than almost every nucleated cell.
optionExplanations: Most nucleated cells express class I rather than constitutive class II.
Bg markers are associated with class I HLA.
DR,DQ,DP are the class II families.
Platelets do not normally express class II HLA.

quickCheck.question: Which class contains HLA-A,B,C?
quickCheck.answer: Class I.

boc-1-227.questionInPlainEnglish: What routine measurement helps predict stem-cell product engraftment?
boc-1-227.explanation: CD34 marks many blood-forming stem/progenitor cells. Counting CD34-positive cells estimates the effective cell dose, although it does not guarantee successful engraftment.
optionExplanations: Clonogenic assays measure growth but are less routine.
Viability shows living cells but not the specific progenitor dose.
CD34 enumeration is the widely used surrogate measure.
A manual differential cannot reliably count functional stem cells.
boc-1-227.memory: CD34 count estimates the transplant's progenitor dose.

quickCheck.question: What does engraftment mean?
quickCheck.answer: Transplanted cells establish themselves and begin producing blood cells.

boc-1-228.questionInPlainEnglish: What treatment prevents donor-cell graft-versus-host disease during transplant support?
boc-1-228.explanation: Irradiation disables donor T-cell multiplication. Washing, CMV selection, and leukocyte reduction address other risks but do not reliably replace it.
optionExplanations: Irradiation prevents donor T-cell proliferation.
Washing removes plasma rather than disabling all T cells.
CMV-seronegative selection addresses infection risk.
Leukocyte reduction does not guarantee removal of every viable T cell.
boc-1-228.memory: TA-GVHD prevention requires disabling donor T cells.

quickCheck.question: Can approved pathogen reduction also prevent this risk in certain products?
quickCheck.answer: Yes, where the product's approved processing supports that use.

boc-1-229.questionInPlainEnglish: Which stem-cell transplant is major ABO incompatible?
boc-1-229.explanation: Major incompatibility means the recipient has antibodies against donor ABO antigens. An O recipient has anti-B that recognizes B-donor cells.
optionExplanations: O donor plasma may attack A-recipient cells: minor direction.
AB recipient lacks anti-A, so this is not major.
O-recipient anti-B targets the B donor: major incompatibility.
O donor plasma may attack B-recipient cells: minor direction.
boc-1-229.memory: Major: recipient antibodies attack donor antigens.

quickCheck.question: What is minor ABO incompatibility?
quickCheck.answer: Donor antibodies can attack the recipient's ABO antigens.

boc-1-230.questionInPlainEnglish: What guides red-cell selection one day after a major ABO-mismatched stem-cell transplant?
boc-1-230.explanation: Recipient ABO antibodies do not disappear immediately. Early donor red cells must remain compatible with the antibodies still circulating, while the transplant team manages the transition.
optionExplanations: Circulating recipient antibodies determine safe early red-cell selection.
Platelet/plasma choice must consider donor and recipient compatibility.
Immediate donor-identical cells may be attacked by remaining recipient antibody.
AB red cells carry both targets and are not universally safe.
boc-1-230.memory: After transplant, antibody transition takes time.

quickCheck.question: Why not immediately switch red cells to the stem-cell donor's ABO type?
quickCheck.answer: Recipient antibodies may still attack that type.

boc-1-230.sourceNote: Current transplant component algorithms consider both donor and recipient; the source's universal donor-identical plasma wording is oversimplified.

boc-1-231.questionInPlainEnglish: Which ancestry group has higher frequencies of this B, Dce pattern in the source?
boc-1-231.explanation: The source associates B and the Dce phenotype with higher frequencies in Black donor populations. Blood type gives only a population probability, never proof of ethnicity.
optionExplanations: The source gives lower Dce frequency in Asian populations.
Hispanic ancestry is not the source's intended association.
Black populations have the highest cited Dce frequency.
White populations have a lower cited Dce frequency.
boc-1-231.memory: Population frequency is not individual identity.

quickCheck.question: Can blood-group tests determine someone's ethnicity?
quickCheck.answer: No; substantial overlap exists among populations.

boc-1-231.sourceNote: The question uses historical ancestry categories and cannot establish an individual's ethnicity.

boc-1-232.questionInPlainEnglish: What should happen when today's ABO type conflicts with yesterday's?
boc-1-232.explanation: A cannot safely become B overnight under ordinary circumstances. Obtain a correctly identified new specimen and resolve the mismatch before relying on either result.
optionExplanations: Using yesterday's A result may accept a wrong specimen.
Using today's B result may accept a wrong specimen.
AB cells are not universally compatible and do not fix identification.
A new properly identified sample helps resolve the discrepancy.
boc-1-232.memory: Conflicting ABO history demands identity investigation.

quickCheck.question: Why are historical types compared with current results?
quickCheck.answer: To catch collection, identification, or testing errors.

boc-1-233.questionInPlainEnglish: What should happen when a unit labeled D-negative tests strongly D-positive?
boc-1-233.explanation: The unit must be held while its identity and labeling discrepancy are resolved. The collection facility needs notification so it can investigate and correct related records.
optionExplanations: Do not transfuse under a contradicted D-negative label.
Do not independently relabel and use before resolution.
Notify the collecting facility and investigate the mismatch.
Immediate disposal loses material useful for investigation.
boc-1-233.memory: A label/testing mismatch must be resolved before use.

quickCheck.question: Why notify the supplier rather than just change the label?
quickCheck.answer: The mismatch may reflect a broader identity or process error.

boc-1-234.questionInPlainEnglish: Which patient is most likely to have weak expected reverse ABO antibodies?
boc-1-234.explanation: Young children are still developing their usual ABO antibody levels. A two-year-old can show weaker anti-B than an older child's or adult's sample.
optionExplanations: Pregnancy alone does not explain the usual developmental weakness.
A 30-year-old usually has established ABO antibodies.
A two-year-old is still approaching adult antibody levels.
A teenager usually has established ABO antibodies.
boc-1-234.memory: Children's reverse-group antibodies strengthen with age.

quickCheck.question: Why is newborn reverse ABO typing unreliable?
quickCheck.answer: The baby's own ABO antibodies are not yet developed.

boc-1-235.questionInPlainEnglish: Using a 20% compatible frequency, how many units are screened per compatible unit on average?
boc-1-235.explanation: The expected number is 1 divided by 0.20, or five. This is an average, not a promise that every fifth unit will be compatible.
optionExplanations: Five equals 1/0.20, the expected screening number.
Ten corresponds to only 10% compatibility.
Fifteen exceeds the stated average expectation.
Twenty exceeds the stated average expectation.

quickCheck.question: Does screening five units guarantee one compatible unit?
quickCheck.answer: No; random outcomes vary.

boc-1-235.sourceNote: The source's 20% figure likely refers to A2 among group A; many group O or B cells also lack A1.

boc-1-236.questionInPlainEnglish: What anti-A pattern may occur as O donor marrow replaces A recipient cells?
boc-1-236.explanation: Old A cells react with anti-A while new donor-derived O cells do not. This two-population mixture produces mixed-field agglutination.
optionExplanations: Rouleaux is protein-related stacking, not two ABO populations.
Aggregation is too nonspecific for the defined pattern.
Polyagglutination involves unusual broad cell reactivity.
Mixed field describes clumps beside unreacted cells.
boc-1-236.memory: Two cell populations can produce mixed field.

quickCheck.question: Does the marrow transplant instantly replace all circulating red cells?
quickCheck.answer: No; existing recipient cells persist during the transition.

boc-1-237.questionInPlainEnglish: How can a positive DAT interfere with an AHG weak D test?
boc-1-237.explanation: Cells already coated with IgG can react at AHG regardless of D reagent. A positive control therefore invalidates the weak D interpretation.
optionExplanations: A patient's DAT does not necessarily make all donor crossmatches positive.
Both test and control can react from preexisting cell coating.
The serum screen may be negative despite a positive DAT.
ABO forward/reverse grouping need not disagree.
boc-1-237.memory: Positive weak D control means no valid weak D conclusion.

quickCheck.question: Why include a control in weak D testing?
quickCheck.answer: To detect reactivity unrelated to the anti-D reagent.

boc-1-238.questionInPlainEnglish: What disease can cause false ABO clumping that disappears after washing or saline replacement?
boc-1-238.explanation: Excess plasma proteins in multiple myeloma can stack red cells into rouleaux. Removing protein separates stacks, while true antibody agglutination remains.
optionExplanations: Immune deficiency more often weakens expected antibodies.
Agammaglobulinemia means low antibodies, not protein-rich rouleaux.
Myeloma can produce excess proteins causing rouleaux.
Acquired B does not disappear simply through saline replacement.
boc-1-238.memory: Rouleaux resembles coins stacked by excess proteins.

quickCheck.question: What distinguishes rouleaux from true agglutination in saline replacement?
quickCheck.answer: Rouleaux disperses; genuine antibody-linked clumps persist.

boc-1-238.sourceNote: The second table is corrupted; interpretation follows the source's stated saline-resolution pattern.

boc-1-239.questionInPlainEnglish: What ABO appearance can result when bacteria remove an acetyl group from A antigen?
boc-1-239.explanation: Deacetylation changes the A sugar into a B-like structure. Some anti-B reagents then react weakly, creating an acquired B appearance in a group A person.
optionExplanations: Acquired B is the bacterial-modification pattern.
B(A) refers to weak A-like activity in certain B phenotypes.
Amod is not the named deacetylation phenomenon.
Aint is an inherited subgroup pattern, not acquired B.
boc-1-239.memory: Acquired B modifies A; it does not change inherited ABO genes.

quickCheck.question: Does acquired B mean the patient genetically became group B?
quickCheck.answer: No; surface chemistry changed temporarily.

boc-1-240.questionInPlainEnglish: Which gene is most often absent in ordinary D-negative people?
boc-1-240.explanation: RHD encodes D antigen. Deletion of RHD commonly explains D-negative typing, while RHCE remains and produces C/c and E/e antigens.
optionExplanations: Deleting both genes is not the usual D-negative mechanism.
RHCE deletion does not specifically explain ordinary D negativity.
RHD deletion is the common mechanism intended.
Removing both RHD and RHCE is not ordinary D negativity.
boc-1-240.memory: RHD makes D; RHCE makes C/c and E/e.

quickCheck.question: Do D-negative people still have other Rh antigens?
quickCheck.answer: Yes, usually C/c and E/e combinations.

boc-1-240.sourceNote: OCR prints RHD as RHO; D-negative mechanisms differ across populations.

boc-1-241.questionInPlainEnglish: How should unexpected reverse-group B-cell reactivity be investigated?
boc-1-241.explanation: The patient types B but reacts with B reverse cells. An unexpected antibody to a non-ABO marker on those cells may be responsible; group O screening cells help investigate it.
optionExplanations: Treating patient cells does not explain the serum's unexpected reaction.
Anti-A1 investigation is inappropriate for an apparent group B patient.
Washing patient cells addresses forward interference, not this serum reaction.
Screening O cells at cold and AHG phases can reveal another antibody.
boc-1-241.memory: Reverse cells carry non-ABO antigens too.

quickCheck.question: Why can an antibody interfere with reverse typing without being anti-A or anti-B?
quickCheck.answer: The reagent cells also express other blood-group antigens.

boc-1-242.questionInPlainEnglish: What reagent first binds red cells in a weak D test?
boc-1-242.explanation: Anti-D is incubated with cells so even small D amounts can bind antibody. AHG later reveals the attached IgG; there is no separate anti-Du reagent.
optionExplanations: Different dilutions are not the defining test procedure.
Anti-D binds any detectable weak D sites.
Du is an older term, not a separate antigen reagent.
AHG comes after anti-D incubation and washing.
boc-1-242.memory: Weak D uses anti-D followed by an antiglobulin phase.

quickCheck.question: What does AHG reveal in weak D testing?
quickCheck.answer: Anti-D already attached to the red cells.

boc-1-243.questionInPlainEnglish: What explains O-like forward typing but A-like reverse typing?
boc-1-243.explanation: A weak A subgroup may have too little A for routine anti-A detection. Its plasma still lacks expected anti-A and contains anti-B, giving A-like reverse results.
optionExplanations: Rouleaux would not specifically explain the absent A1 reaction.
Acquired B should produce unexpected anti-B forward reactivity.
Bombay usually has strong anti-H and broader reverse reactions.
A weak A subgroup explains hidden A with A-like serum.
boc-1-243.memory: Weak A may hide in forward typing.

quickCheck.question: How can very weak A be demonstrated?
quickCheck.answer: Specialized adsorption and elution or other subgroup investigation.

boc-1-244.questionInPlainEnglish: What can be inferred about a D-positive father of a D-negative baby?
boc-1-244.explanation: The father must be able to pass a non-D-producing version. A D-positive father carrying one D and one non-D package fits a D-negative child.
optionExplanations: A homozygous D father would pass D to every child in this model.
A D-negative mother does not carry an expressed ordinary D allele.
A heterozygous D father can pass his non-D package.
The inheritance pattern is possible without a typing error.
boc-1-244.memory: A D-positive parent can have a D-negative child if heterozygous.

quickCheck.question: Which parental contribution produces a D-negative baby in this simplified model?
quickCheck.answer: A non-D-producing package from each parent.

boc-1-245.questionInPlainEnglish: What enables certain antibodies to rupture target red cells in a test tube?
boc-1-245.explanation: Complement is a protein cascade that can build membrane pores after antibody binds. That causes hemolysis, releasing red hemoglobin into the surrounding fluid.
optionExplanations: Complement supplies the cascade capable of cell lysis.
Anticoagulants prevent clotting and do not supply lytic complement.
Preservatives maintain cells rather than activate specific hemolysis.
Penicillin matters only in particular drug-dependent mechanisms.
boc-1-245.memory: Antibody plus target plus complement can cause lysis.

quickCheck.question: What visible clue can indicate hemolysis?
quickCheck.answer: A pink or red supernatant from released hemoglobin.

boc-1-246.questionInPlainEnglish: What comes next after a positive AHG antibody screen?
boc-1-246.explanation: Agglutination indicates a reacting antibody or other interference. Identification testing establishes what caused it so suitable donor cells can be selected.
optionExplanations: Check cells validate negative, not already positive, AHG tests.
Identify the cause of the positive reaction.
Elution is for antibody attached to cells, not this first serum step.
DAT alone does not identify the serum antibody.
boc-1-246.memory: Positive screen leads to antibody investigation.

quickCheck.question: Why identify an antibody rather than just label the screen positive?
quickCheck.answer: Its target determines which donor antigens must be avoided.

boc-1-247.questionInPlainEnglish: What most likely causes AHG positivity in both screening cells and the patient's own cells?
boc-1-247.explanation: A warm autoantibody recognizes a widely shared self antigen. It therefore reacts with both donor screening cells and the autocontrol at AHG.
optionExplanations: Rouleaux is usually resolved by appropriate washing or replacement.
Warm self-reactivity fits positive screen and autocontrol.
Cold antibodies more typically react at earlier, cooler phases.
Multiple alloantibodies do not usually explain self-cell reactivity.
boc-1-247.memory: AHG panreactivity plus positive auto suggests warm autoantibody.

quickCheck.question: What does a positive autocontrol show?
quickCheck.answer: The patient's plasma reacts with their own tested red cells.

boc-1-248.questionInPlainEnglish: Why are screening cells and only two of six donor units AHG-incompatible?
boc-1-248.explanation: An alloantibody targets an antigen on some donors but not others. The two reactive units likely carry the target; the other four may lack it.
optionExplanations: A recipient alloantibody explains selective donor incompatibility.
An autoantibody would more often react broadly with all donors.
Two positive donor DATs do not explain both screening-cell reactions well.
A recipient DAT does not itself cause selective donor-cell reactions.
boc-1-248.memory: Selective donor reactions suggest an alloantigen pattern.

quickCheck.question: Why can four donors be compatible while the screen is positive?
quickCheck.answer: Those donors may lack the detected antibody's antigen.

boc-1-249.questionInPlainEnglish: Which condition fits anemia, high reticulocytes, IgG DAT, and self-reactive AHG testing?
boc-1-249.explanation: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia causes IgG coating and destruction of the person's red cells. Marrow responds by releasing more young red cells, called reticulocytes.
optionExplanations: Cold disease more often produces complement-dominant DAT findings.
Warm AIHA fits IgG coating, self-reactivity, and hemolysis.
Drug-dependent penicillin antibodies require supporting drug evidence.
A delayed alloimmune reaction would not usually produce this broad self-reactivity.
boc-1-249.memory: Anemia plus high reticulocytes suggests increased red-cell loss.

quickCheck.question: What does a high reticulocyte count show here?
quickCheck.answer: The marrow is trying to replace destroyed red cells.

boc-1-250.questionInPlainEnglish: What additional check is requested before accepting all-positive forward typing?
boc-1-250.explanation: If anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D all react, nonspecific cell reactivity could imitate AB D-positive. A suitable negative control helps establish that the reagent reactions are specific.
optionExplanations: AB D-positive is plausible but the source requires a control first.
A subgroup is not demonstrated by uniformly strong reactions.
Repeat with an appropriate control to check nonspecific reactivity.
Extra room-temperature incubation does not address the control question.
boc-1-250.memory: All reactive tests need a way to exclude nonspecific reactions.

quickCheck.question: What does a positive inert control mean?
quickCheck.answer: The typing reactions cannot be accepted as specific.

boc-1-250.sourceNote: Control requirements depend on the reagents and validated method; follow manufacturer instructions.

boc-1-251.questionInPlainEnglish: What does a major crossmatch test?
boc-1-251.explanation: Recipient plasma is mixed with donor red cells. It asks whether recipient antibodies can attack antigens on that particular donor's cells.
optionExplanations: An A patient given O cells may still crossmatch compatibly.
Donor plasma antibodies are not the major crossmatch target.
A D-negative donor mislabeled positive may still crossmatch compatibly.
Recipient antibody against donor red-cell antigens is what it detects.
boc-1-251.memory: Major crossmatch: recipient plasma plus donor cells.

quickCheck.question: Whose serum is used in the major crossmatch?
quickCheck.answer: The recipient's serum or plasma.

boc-1-252.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed cause can make an AHG crossmatch incompatible?
boc-1-252.explanation: Donor cells already coated with IgG can react with AHG even without an antibody in recipient plasma. A donor DAT checks this possibility.
optionExplanations: Recipient-cell rare antigens are not present in this donor-cell test.
Donor serum is not being tested in the major crossmatch.
Recipient polyagglutinable cells are not the cells used here.
A positive donor DAT can cause the AHG incompatibility.
boc-1-252.memory: Unexpected AHG donor reaction: consider donor DAT.

quickCheck.question: Can a negative recipient screen guarantee every donor crossmatch is negative?
quickCheck.answer: No; donor coating or rare donor antigens can cause exceptions.

boc-1-253.questionInPlainEnglish: Which antibody best fits reactions only at immediate spin and room temperature?
boc-1-253.explanation: Lewis antibodies are commonly IgM and cold-reactive. Anti-Lea fits the disappearance of reactions at 37°C and AHG better than the listed IgG antibodies.
optionExplanations: Anti-Jkb usually reacts at the antiglobulin phase.
Anti-Lea commonly reacts at cooler direct-agglutination phases.
Anti-C is usually clinically important IgG at AHG.
Anti-Fya is usually clinically important IgG at AHG.
boc-1-253.memory: Cold-only direct reaction suggests IgM such as Lewis.

quickCheck.question: Why record the phase of each antibody reaction?
quickCheck.answer: It helps distinguish cold from body-temperature-reactive antibodies.

boc-1-254.questionInPlainEnglish: What DNA differences do blood-group arrays commonly detect?
boc-1-254.explanation: A SNP is a single-letter difference in DNA. Such differences can predict changes in blood-group proteins after the relevant DNA regions are amplified.
optionExplanations: A stop codon is one possible sequence feature, not the general answer.
mRNA is a transcript, not the genomic target described.
SNPs are the DNA sequence differences commonly examined.
cDNA is copied from RNA, not the genomic DNA described.

quickCheck.question: Is DNA made of amino acids?
quickCheck.answer: No; DNA is made of nucleotides.

boc-1-254.sourceNote: The stem incorrectly calls DNA residues amino acids and implies arrays directly detect protein changes; they detect DNA variants.

boc-1-255.questionInPlainEnglish: Which available red cells best suit an AB, D-negative patient in this comparison?
boc-1-255.explanation: AB recipients usually lack anti-A and anti-B, allowing group A cells. D-negative group A cells preserve D matching while conserving group O inventory.
optionExplanations: AB D-positive exposes a D-negative patient to D.
A D-negative is ABO-compatible and avoids D exposure.
A D-positive is ABO-compatible but supplies D.
O D-negative is compatible but the source conserves O for those needing it.
boc-1-255.memory: AB recipients can receive A red cells if other checks permit.

quickCheck.question: Why can AB recipients receive group A red cells?
quickCheck.answer: They ordinarily have no anti-A.

boc-1-255.sourceNote: Emergency decisions depend on current protocols, inventory, and patient factors.

boc-1-256.questionInPlainEnglish: Which available red cells avoid clinically reactive anti-A1 in an A2B, D-positive patient?
boc-1-256.explanation: Group B cells lack A1 and are ABO-compatible with an AB patient. D-positive units also avoid unnecessarily using scarce D-negative stock.
optionExplanations: B D-positive lacks A1 and fits the patient's D status.
B D-negative could fit but uses D-negative inventory unnecessarily here.
A1B carries the target of the patient's anti-A1.
O D-negative may fit but is not the source's first choice.

quickCheck.question: Why is A1B unsuitable despite being an AB type?
quickCheck.answer: It carries A1, which this patient's antibody recognizes.

boc-1-257.questionInPlainEnglish: What error can an overly concentrated red-cell suspension cause?
boc-1-257.explanation: Too many cells spread a limited antibody amount across too many antigen sites. This antigen-excess effect can weaken clumping and create a false negative.
optionExplanations: Antigen excess tends to weaken reactions, not create this false positive.
Prozone is antibody excess, not a heavy cell suspension.
Antibody excess is the wrong mechanism for too many cells.
Antigen excess can dilute antibody coating enough to miss a reaction.
boc-1-257.memory: Too many cells can hide weak antibody.

quickCheck.question: What term describes antibody excess instead?
quickCheck.answer: Prozone.

boc-1-258.questionInPlainEnglish: What extra test helps investigate multiple antibodies after a remote transfusion?
boc-1-258.explanation: Phenotyping the patient's own cells identifies antigens they possess and lack. That narrows possible alloantibodies because people ordinarily form them against absent antigens.
optionExplanations: Phenotyping helps focus the alloantibody investigation.
Friends or relatives are not automatically more compatible donors.
Treating patient cells does not directly identify serum specificities.
Patient serum is not a validated antigen-typing reagent.
boc-1-258.memory: Know the patient's antigen profile to narrow possible antibodies.

quickCheck.question: Why does recent transfusion complicate phenotyping?
quickCheck.answer: Mixed donor and patient cells can give misleading antigen results.

boc-1-259.questionInPlainEnglish: Which system most often gives recognizable warm autoantibody specificity?
boc-1-259.explanation: Warm autoantibodies often react broadly, sometimes with Rh-related preferences. Cold autoantibodies more commonly involve I or P-associated patterns.
optionExplanations: Rh is the classic warm-autoantibody association.
I is more associated with cold autoantibodies.
P is associated with PCH rather than usual warm AIHA.
Duffy specificity is an uncommon warm-autoantibody example.
boc-1-259.memory: Warm autoantibodies often show Rh-related reactivity.

quickCheck.question: Does every warm autoantibody have a clean single Rh specificity?
quickCheck.answer: No; many are broadly reactive.

boc-1-260.questionInPlainEnglish: Which antibody best fits in-vitro hemolysis with only some donor units?
boc-1-260.explanation: Anti-Lea can activate complement and lyse Lea-positive cells in fresh serum. Its target is present on only a minority of donors, fitting selective reactions.
optionExplanations: Anti-Lea can produce complement-mediated in-vitro hemolysis.
Anti-s is not the classic lytic example here.
k is very common, so only three reactive donors would be unexpected.
Anti-E usually does not produce this characteristic in-vitro hemolysis.
boc-1-260.memory: Lewis antibodies can occasionally be hemolytic.

quickCheck.question: Why might fresh serum matter for this reaction?
quickCheck.answer: It supplies active complement.

boc-1-261.questionInPlainEnglish: Which antigen cannot yet be excluded as this panel's antibody target?
boc-1-261.explanation: A nonreactive cell can exclude targets it expresses, subject to dosage and method. Here the nonreactive cells cover antigens 2–5 but not antigen 1.
optionExplanations: Antigen 1 remains consistent with the reacting-cell pattern.
Antigen 2 appears on a nonreactive cell, allowing exclusion here.
Antigen 3 appears on a nonreactive cell, allowing exclusion here.
Antigen 4 appears on a nonreactive cell, allowing exclusion here.
boc-1-261.memory: Rule out with nonreactive antigen-positive cells.

quickCheck.question: Why not rule out an antigen using a negative cell that lacks it?
quickCheck.answer: That cell never offered the antibody a target.

boc-1-261.sourceNote: The extracted panel is badly misaligned; this explanation follows the source's rule-out description.

boc-1-262.questionInPlainEnglish: Which pair remains possible after this panel's rule-outs?
boc-1-262.explanation: Nonreactive cells eliminate K, P1, M and Jka in the source interpretation. Anti-c and anti-E remain possible and require suitable additional cells to separate them.
optionExplanations: M and K are excluded by nonreactive target-positive cells.
c and E remain possible after the stated rule-outs.
Jka is excluded even though c remains possible.
P1 is excluded even though c remains possible.
boc-1-262.memory: A panel can leave more than one specificity possible.

quickCheck.question: Does a remaining possibility prove both antibodies are present?
quickCheck.answer: No; additional discriminating cells are needed.

boc-1-262.sourceNote: The extracted antigen table is misaligned; verify against the original panel.

boc-1-263.questionInPlainEnglish: Which common antibody has NOT been ruled out here?
boc-1-263.explanation: The negative cells express C, Leb and Jka, so those antibodies can be excluded under the source's conditions. E remains possible because the relevant E-positive cells react.
optionExplanations: C is present on nonreactive cells and is excluded.
Leb is present on nonreactive cells and is excluded.
Jka is present on nonreactive cells and is excluded.
E remains compatible with the reaction pattern.
boc-1-263.memory: Not ruled out means possible, not proven.

quickCheck.question: What would help confirm anti-E?
quickCheck.answer: Additional suitable E-positive and E-negative cells plus patient antigen testing.

boc-1-263.sourceNote: The source panel extraction is heavily misaligned.

boc-1-264.questionInPlainEnglish: What syndrome is suggested by broad antibody reactivity, negative DAT, and weak Kell expression?
boc-1-264.explanation: McLeod cells lack Kx and express Kell antigens weakly. Affected patients may have acanthocytes and associated problems; certain linked deletions also cause recurrent-infection syndromes.
optionExplanations: PCH usually involves complement coating and a different testing pattern.
McLeod syndrome fits weakened Kell and the clinical clues.
Warm AIHA usually has a positive IgG DAT.
Cold agglutinin disease usually has complement DAT and cold reactivity.

quickCheck.question: Why can McLeod cells lead to broad antibody problems?
quickCheck.answer: They lack antigens present on most ordinary donor cells.

boc-1-264.sourceNote: The phenotype table is misaligned. CGD association is specific to some linked genetic deletions, not every McLeod case.

boc-1-265.questionInPlainEnglish: What emergency red cells are preferred before current typing in this adolescent?
boc-1-265.explanation: The source selects uncrossmatched O D-negative cells while testing proceeds. This avoids uncertain ABO identity and limits D sensitization risk in a young D-negative patient.
optionExplanations: Old A records do not replace current specimen verification here.
O D-negative is the preferred emergency-release product listed.
O D-positive creates avoidable D exposure in this scenario.
Withholding lifesaving blood until typing finishes is inappropriate.
boc-1-265.memory: Emergency release uses current protocol while testing continues.

quickCheck.question: Why are group O cells used before ABO is confirmed?
quickCheck.answer: They lack A and B red-cell antigens.

boc-1-265.sourceNote: Educational emergency comparison; actual release follows institutional massive-transfusion policy.

boc-1-266.questionInPlainEnglish: What is the usual red-cell effect of transfusing Ch-positive cells to someone with anti-Ch?
boc-1-266.explanation: Chido antibodies usually do not shorten red-cell survival. Their antigen is carried by plasma complement protein deposited on cells, rather than a typical intrinsic red-cell target.
optionExplanations: No clinically important red-cell destruction is the usual outcome.
Significant immune hemolysis is not the usual anti-Ch behavior.
Reduced chromium-labeled survival is not the expected finding.
Fever is not the defining effect of anti-Ch.
boc-1-266.memory: Anti-Ch often complicates testing without causing red-cell hemolysis.

quickCheck.question: Can a difficult antibody panel involve a clinically insignificant antibody?
quickCheck.answer: Yes; laboratory interference and clinical harm are different issues.

boc-1-267.questionInPlainEnglish: Which antibody combination best explains this multi-phase panel?
boc-1-267.explanation: The source excludes M and Leb using nonreactive cells carrying those targets. The remaining reaction pattern is consistent with E, Jka and K antibodies together.
optionExplanations: M is excluded, so this combination does not fit.
E,Jka,K together explain the remaining source pattern.
M is excluded even though Jka remains possible.
Leb is excluded even though E remains possible.
boc-1-267.memory: Multiple antibodies create overlapping reaction patterns.

quickCheck.question: Why use carefully selected cells after a screening panel?
quickCheck.answer: To separate overlapping specificities.

boc-1-267.sourceNote: The extracted panel is misaligned; confirm detailed cell-by-cell interpretation from the original.

boc-1-268.questionInPlainEnglish: What do anti-Fya, anti-Jka, and anti-K have in common?
boc-1-268.explanation: All are typically clinically important IgG antibodies detected at IAT. They can harm transfused cells and, because IgG crosses the placenta, may cause fetal/newborn disease.
optionExplanations: IAT detection and potential HDFN/transfusion reactions fit all three.
Enzymes destroy Fya but not all three targets.
All three can cause HDFN, despite differing frequency and severity.
Room-temperature detection is not their characteristic shared phase.

quickCheck.question: Why can these antibodies affect a fetus?
quickCheck.answer: Their IgG form can cross the placenta.

boc-1-269.questionInPlainEnglish: Which antibody fits selective AHG reactivity strengthened by enzymes?
boc-1-269.explanation: Rh antibodies often become stronger with enzyme-treated cells. Nonreactive cells exclude D, E and K in the source, leaving anti-C.
optionExplanations: Anti-C fits the reactive cells and enzyme enhancement.
E is excluded by an E-positive nonreactive cell.
D is excluded by a D-positive nonreactive cell.
K is excluded and is not characteristically enzyme-enhanced.
boc-1-269.memory: Enzyme enhancement supports Rh or Kidd possibilities.

quickCheck.question: Do stronger enzyme reactions alone identify anti-C?
quickCheck.answer: No; the antigen pattern must also match.

boc-1-269.sourceNote: The extracted table is misaligned; use the original for detailed rule-outs.

boc-1-270.questionInPlainEnglish: Can the antibody identified in this prenatal panel cause HDFN?
boc-1-270.explanation: The source identifies anti-Fya. Its IgG form can cross the placenta and damage fetal Fya-positive cells, with severity ranging from mild to occasionally severe.
optionExplanations: Fatal disease is not the usual expected outcome.
Anti-Fya may cause HDFN, the correct risk statement.
It is not safe to dismiss anti-Fya as unrelated to HDFN.
The source's pattern supports a specificity rather than no interpretation.
boc-1-270.memory: IgG anti-Fya can affect fetal cells.

quickCheck.question: What additional fetal feature determines whether anti-Fya has a target?
quickCheck.answer: Whether the fetus expresses Fya.

boc-1-270.sourceNote: The extracted panel is misaligned; anti-Fya identification follows the source rationale.

boc-1-271.questionInPlainEnglish: Which test detects antibodies already attached to red cells inside the patient?
boc-1-271.explanation: The direct antiglobulin test examines the patient's washed cells for IgG or complement coating acquired in vivo. It differs from testing free serum antibodies.
optionExplanations: DAT detects preexisting red-cell coating.
Complement fixation is not the routine test described.
IAT creates antibody binding during laboratory incubation.
Immunofluorescence is not the usual routine method here.
boc-1-271.memory: DAT is direct evidence of cell coating.

quickCheck.question: Does a positive DAT by itself prove active hemolysis?
quickCheck.answer: No; evidence of cell destruction must also be assessed.

boc-1-272.questionInPlainEnglish: Why can anti-I cold disease produce a positive DAT?
boc-1-272.explanation: Cold IgM may detach when blood warms, leaving complement fragments behind. C3d coating is then detected by the DAT.
optionExplanations: Visible cold clumping is not itself what DAT reagent detects.
C3d remains on cells and is detected by anti-C3d.
T activation is a different membrane modification.
C3d, rather than the stated C3c, is the usual persistent marker.
boc-1-272.memory: Cold antibody can leave a complement footprint.

quickCheck.question: Why may IgM be absent from a positive DAT in cold disease?
quickCheck.answer: It may detach on warming while complement remains.

boc-1-273.questionInPlainEnglish: Which DAT pattern suggests a delayed serologic reaction after transfusion?
boc-1-273.explanation: Only transfused donor cells may carry the newly detected antibody's target. A mixed-field DAT therefore fits a coated donor subpopulation among uncoated recipient cells.
optionExplanations: Result A is intended to show the mixed-field pattern.
Complement-only uniform reactivity is less specific for the mixed population.
Uniform IgG positivity does not specifically show donor-only coating.
Strong uniform IgG/C3 positivity does not show the intended mixture.
boc-1-273.memory: Delayed serologic reaction may reveal coating without symptoms.

quickCheck.question: How does a serologic reaction differ from a hemolytic reaction?
quickCheck.answer: Serologic findings occur without demonstrated clinically significant red-cell destruction.

boc-1-273.sourceNote: Result A's mixed-field entries are lost in extraction; the original table is required to verify its appearance.

boc-1-274.questionInPlainEnglish: Which cells react most strongly with dosage-sensitive anti-M?
boc-1-274.explanation: M+N− cells usually carry two M alleles and express more M than M+N+ cells. More available target can make a weak anti-M easier to detect.
optionExplanations: M-negative cells provide no M target.
M+N+ cells have only one ordinary M allele.
M+N− cells provide the strongest double-dose M expression.
M+N+ remains heterozygous despite its S/s status.
boc-1-274.memory: For anti-M dosage, look for M+N−.

quickCheck.question: Do S and s results determine M dosage here?
quickCheck.answer: No; M/N expression is the relevant pair.

boc-1-275.questionInPlainEnglish: What does AHG do in the direct antiglobulin test?
boc-1-275.explanation: AHG binds human IgG or complement already coating the patient's red cells. Its bridging action makes that otherwise invisible coating detectable.
optionExplanations: AHG does not supply complement to lyse indicator cells.
Precipitating free antibody is not the DAT's purpose.
DAT is not a complement-fixation serum assay.
It detects preexisting antibody or complement on erythrocytes.
boc-1-275.memory: AHG reveals coating already present on cells.

quickCheck.question: What is an erythrocyte?
quickCheck.answer: A red blood cell.

boc-1-276.questionInPlainEnglish: How does penicillin classically cause immune red-cell destruction?
boc-1-276.explanation: Penicillin can stick tightly to red-cell proteins. Anti-penicillin antibodies then recognize the drug-coated cell, marking it for destruction.
optionExplanations: Drug-coated-cell recognition is the classic penicillin mechanism.
Drug present only in fluid is a different testing mechanism.
Drug-independent autoantibodies are classically linked to other drugs.
Nonspecific protein adsorption is not this antibody-mediated mechanism.
boc-1-276.memory: Penicillin can become the target attached to a red cell.

quickCheck.question: Why test penicillin-treated cells for this antibody?
quickCheck.answer: Untreated cells do not carry its drug target.

boc-1-277.questionInPlainEnglish: How does EDTA stop classical complement activation in a sample?
boc-1-277.explanation: EDTA binds calcium so it is unavailable. Calcium is needed to maintain the C1 complex that initiates classical complement activation.
optionExplanations: Rapid spontaneous decay is not EDTA's main mechanism.
Magnesium binding does not explain the stated C6 assembly claim.
Calcium removal prevents functional C1 assembly.
Chemotaxis is cell movement, not the initial complement step.
boc-1-277.memory: EDTA traps calcium and stops C1.

quickCheck.question: Why is EDTA helpful for a DAT specimen?
quickCheck.answer: It limits complement attachment occurring after collection.

boc-1-278.questionInPlainEnglish: What is antibody-independent protein coating caused by certain drugs called?
boc-1-278.explanation: Some drugs change the red-cell surface so plasma proteins stick nonspecifically. This can give a positive DAT without a specific anti-drug antibody.
optionExplanations: Drug-dependent antibody requires a specific antibody, unlike this process.
Complement-dependent drug antibody is a different mechanism.
A drug-induced autoantibody is still antibody-mediated.
Nonimmunologic protein adsorption describes nonspecific sticking.
boc-1-278.memory: Positive DAT does not always mean specific immune hemolysis.

quickCheck.question: Can nonspecific drug-related protein coating occur without hemolysis?
quickCheck.answer: Yes; coating and clinically important destruction are different findings.

boc-1-278.sourceNote: Cephalosporins can also cause genuine antibody-mediated hemolysis; this item describes one mechanism only.

boc-1-279.questionInPlainEnglish: What fraction of units usually lack low-prevalence Kpa?
boc-1-279.explanation: Kpa occurs in only about 1–2% of the source populations. Therefore almost all random units lack it and are potentially compatible with anti-Kpa.
optionExplanations: Less than 2% describes antigen-positive, not compatible units.
50% greatly underestimates Kpa-negative donors.
85% is below the stated Kpa-negative frequency.
About 98% or more lack the target antigen.
boc-1-279.memory: Rare antigen means common antigen-negative blood.

quickCheck.question: Why might anti-Kpa escape a routine screen?
quickCheck.answer: The screening cells may all lack Kpa.

boc-1-279.sourceNote: The source rounds population frequencies; exactly 2% positive corresponds to 98%, not strictly greater than 98%.

boc-1-280.questionInPlainEnglish: Why use anti-A,B during ABO subgroup investigation?
boc-1-280.explanation: Some weak A cells react better with anti-A,B than anti-A alone. This reagent can reveal low-level A expression missed during routine forward typing.
optionExplanations: Anti-A1 is a serum antibody, not what this cell reagent detects.
Anti-A2 is not the intended reagent target.
Weak A subgroups may be detected more readily.
Ordinary O cells have no A/B antigen for this reagent.
boc-1-280.memory: Anti-A,B can expose hidden weak A.

quickCheck.question: Which weak A subgroup often reacts better with anti-A,B?
quickCheck.answer: Ax.

boc-1-281.questionInPlainEnglish: Where might compatible infant red cells come from when the mother has anti-Vel?
boc-1-281.explanation: The mother lacks Vel and therefore can supply Vel-negative cells. Most random and paternal units carry Vel, so specialized donor selection is necessary.
optionExplanations: Maternal cells lack Vel, the target of her antibody.
Paternal cells likely carry common Vel antigen.
Random ABO-matched cells are usually Vel-positive.
O D-negative cells are still usually Vel-positive.
boc-1-281.memory: ABO and D matching do not remove a Vel target.

quickCheck.question: Why wash maternal red cells before using them for the infant?
quickCheck.answer: To remove plasma containing maternal anti-Vel.

boc-1-281.sourceNote: Maternal donation requires full eligibility assessment and applicable neonatal processing including irradiation; this is a source-selection concept.

boc-1-282.questionInPlainEnglish: How can a suspected antibody to typing-reagent additives be investigated?
boc-1-282.explanation: Washing removes the patient's plasma from the cell suspension. If that plasma contains an antibody to an anti-B reagent additive, washing can remove the misleading reaction.
optionExplanations: Anti-A1 lectin does not remove plasma antibody to additives.
Washing and repeating forward typing can remove the interference.
Anti-A,B does not specifically establish additive-dependent reactivity.
A2 reverse cells do not address the false forward anti-B reaction.
boc-1-282.memory: Remove plasma to investigate reagent-dependent false typing.

quickCheck.question: Why can changing reagent brand help?
quickCheck.answer: The alternate reagent may lack the interfering additive.

boc-1-283.questionInPlainEnglish: What does persistent clumping after saline replacement mean?
boc-1-283.explanation: Saline disperses protein-driven rouleaux stacks. If the clumps remain, true antibody-mediated agglutination is more likely than rouleaux.
optionExplanations: Rouleaux should disperse rather than remain.
Persistence alone does not make a properly performed test invalid.
Remaining clumps support true agglutination.
A persistent reaction cannot simply be called negative.

quickCheck.question: What causes rouleaux?
quickCheck.answer: Excess plasma proteins promote red-cell stacking.

boc-1-284.questionInPlainEnglish: Which disorder fits post-infection hemoglobinuria and a positive Donath–Landsteiner test?
boc-1-284.explanation: PCH causes complement-mediated hemolysis after cold binding then warming. Anti-P is supported when P-negative cells resist the test's hemolysis.
optionExplanations: PCH is identified by the biphasic Donath–Landsteiner reaction.
PNH is a different complement-sensitivity disorder, not anti-P.
Warm AIHA does not explain this classic biphasic test.
HEMPAS is not the disorder indicated by anti-P-dependent lysis.

quickCheck.question: Why test P-negative cells as a control?
quickCheck.answer: Lack of lysis supports P-specific antibody action.

boc-1-285.questionInPlainEnglish: What additional identifying information belongs on a transfusion request?
boc-1-285.explanation: The request must identify the authorized person ordering transfusion. Clear patient identifiers and product specifications are also essential to prevent errors.
optionExplanations: Component ABO is selected after compatibility assessment, not this required requester item.
The ordering clinician or authorized professional must be named.
Prior test dates do not replace identifying the prescriber.
Nursing team identity is not the required ordering authority.
boc-1-285.memory: A complete order identifies patient, product, and authorized requester.

quickCheck.question: Why are two independent patient identifiers needed?
quickCheck.answer: To reduce the risk of assigning blood to the wrong person.

boc-1-286.questionInPlainEnglish: What should happen to a transfusion request with unreadable patient identifiers?
boc-1-286.explanation: A legible birth date alone does not securely identify the patient. Obtain a complete, readable request before routine product issue.
optionExplanations: Historical blood type cannot repair an unidentified request.
Transplant status does not waive reliable identification.
Reject and replace the incomplete illegible request.
Apheresis platelets are a valid product; identification is the problem.
boc-1-286.memory: One readable identifier is not enough.

quickCheck.question: Why is relying on a familiar clinical history unsafe?
quickCheck.answer: More than one patient may share similar history or demographics.

boc-1-287.questionInPlainEnglish: Which reagents form a standard adult ABO forward and reverse group?
boc-1-287.explanation: Anti-A and anti-B test the patient's red-cell antigens. A1 and B reagent cells test the patient's expected plasma antibodies, giving an independent cross-check.
optionExplanations: Anti-A,B without separate anti-A/anti-B is not this standard set.
A2 cells are an investigation tool, not routinely required.
Anti-A,anti-B,A1 cells,B cells form the standard set.
Extra anti-A,B and A2 are not routinely required here.
boc-1-287.memory: Forward tests cells; reverse tests plasma.

quickCheck.question: Why should forward and reverse groups agree?
quickCheck.answer: They check complementary sides of the ABO relationship.

boc-1-288.questionInPlainEnglish: When does the source's three-day sample validity end after Tuesday collection?
boc-1-288.explanation: Tuesday is day zero, Wednesday day one, Thursday day two, and Friday day three. Under the stated calendar-day policy the sample expires Friday at 11:59 PM.
optionExplanations: Wednesday is only day one, earlier than required.
Thursday is day two, earlier than required.
Friday 11:59 PM ends day three.
Saturday afternoon exceeds the stated calendar-day rule.
boc-1-288.memory: Collection day counts as day zero.

quickCheck.question: Why shorten specimen validity after recent exposure or unknown history?
quickCheck.answer: New clinically important antibodies may develop.

boc-1-288.sourceNote: This uses the book's calendar-day policy; local standards may specify different timing.

boc-1-289.questionInPlainEnglish: What is the main purpose of an immediate-spin crossmatch?
boc-1-289.explanation: Recipient plasma and donor cells are mixed briefly to detect strong ABO incompatibility. This method does not replace screening for clinically important IgG antibodies.
optionExplanations: Many important IgG antibodies need an antiglobulin method.
Detecting ABO incompatibility is its main purpose.
A compatible result cannot prove the correct patient was sampled.
Detecting all IgM alloantibodies is not its validated primary aim.
boc-1-289.memory: Immediate spin mainly checks ABO compatibility.

quickCheck.question: When is an AHG crossmatch needed instead?
quickCheck.answer: When indicated by clinically significant antibody history or current findings.

boc-1-290.questionInPlainEnglish: What antibody condition permits an electronic crossmatch?
boc-1-290.explanation: A validated computer system can check ABO compatibility when no clinically important antibodies are present or historically recorded. Other identification and validation requirements still apply.
optionExplanations: A historical type alone does not establish full eligibility.
A manual statement is insufficient without validated safeguards.
No current or historical significant alloantibody is essential.
A physical immediate-spin crossmatch is not required merely to duplicate electronic testing.
boc-1-290.memory: Electronic crossmatch needs negative significant-antibody history.

quickCheck.question: Does an undetectable historical antibody still matter?
quickCheck.answer: Yes; past clinically significant antibodies remain relevant.

boc-1-291.questionInPlainEnglish: Can a returned red-cell unit at 12°C be routinely returned to stock under the book's rule?
boc-1-291.explanation: Twelve degrees exceeds the acceptable cold transport range. An intact bag and short elapsed time do not by themselves establish suitability for reissue.
optionExplanations: Previous issue alone is not an automatic discard reason.
Failed temperature requirements are the stated reason to reject reissue.
An intact closure does not correct the temperature excursion.
Good appearance and segments do not prove proper temperature.
boc-1-291.memory: Returned units must meet temperature as well as integrity rules.

quickCheck.question: Why does appearance alone fail to establish safety?
quickCheck.answer: Temperature-related damage or bacterial growth may be invisible.

boc-1-291.sourceNote: Disposition follows validated excursion policy; the source simplifies this to discard.

boc-1-292.questionInPlainEnglish: What are the two essential identity steps when drawing a compatibility specimen?
boc-1-292.explanation: Confirm the patient's identity before drawing, then label the tube immediately at that patient's bedside. These linked steps prevent a correctly tested sample being assigned to the wrong person.
optionExplanations: Vital signs do not replace immediate specimen labeling.
Labeling matters, but identity must be checked before collection.
Identify first and label immediately after collection at bedside.
Reason for transfusion does not replace identity verification.
boc-1-292.memory: Identify, collect, label at the bedside.

quickCheck.question: Why avoid labeling later away from the patient?
quickCheck.answer: Tubes can be mixed up between collection and labeling.

boc-1-293.questionInPlainEnglish: Which recipient detail must appear on the issued unit's compatibility tag?
boc-1-293.explanation: Two independent recipient identifiers connect the selected unit to the intended patient. The tag also links the component identification and compatibility interpretation.
optionExplanations: Two recipient identifiers help prevent wrong-patient transfusion.
Testing staff identity does not replace recipient identification.
Specimen collection date does not identify the recipient sufficiently.
Issue timing does not replace two patient identifiers.
boc-1-293.memory: The tag links this unit to this patient.

quickCheck.question: Why check the tag again at the bedside?
quickCheck.answer: Final identity errors can occur after laboratory testing.

boc-1-294.questionInPlainEnglish: What is a classic nontransfusion cause of mixed-field anti-A reactions?
boc-1-294.explanation: A3 cells characteristically show clumps among unagglutinated cells. Other causes of mixed populations should still be considered, but A3 is the listed subgroup clue.
optionExplanations: Bombay cells lack A and do not give this classic pattern.
T activation causes another type of broad cell reactivity.
A3 is the classic mixed-field A subgroup.
A positive IAT does not itself create mixed-field forward ABO typing.

quickCheck.question: What else can create mixed-field ABO typing?
quickCheck.answer: Transfusion, transplantation, or chimerism can create two cell populations.

boc-1-295.questionInPlainEnglish: What antibody is characteristic of the rare p phenotype?
boc-1-295.explanation: People with p cells lack P, P1 and Pk structures. They can form anti-PP1Pk that reacts strongly with nearly all ordinary donor cells while sparing their own.
optionExplanations: Anti-IP1 is not the characteristic combined antibody.
P2 is a phenotype term, not the intended antibody target.
Anti-PP1Pk is the characteristic clinically important specificity.
Anti-P1 alone does not explain the p phenotype's broad reactivity.
boc-1-295.memory: Rare p cells can make anti-PP1Pk.

quickCheck.question: Why is the autocontrol negative despite broad donor reactivity?
quickCheck.answer: The patient's own cells lack the target antigens.

boc-1-296.questionInPlainEnglish: Which Rh genotype fits D+, C−, E+, c+, e+, f+?
boc-1-296.explanation: R2 supplies DcE and r supplies dce. This combination provides E and e, lacks C, and carries ce together in r so f is present.
optionExplanations: R1R1 expresses C and lacks E/c.
R2R2 lacks e and the ce combination.
R2r matches all listed Rh markers.
R1R2 expresses C and lacks the required f combination.

quickCheck.question: Which package supplies f in R2r?
quickCheck.answer: The r package, because it carries c and e together.

boc-1-297.questionInPlainEnglish: What likely caused a previously negative screen to miss an antibody despite valid check cells?
boc-1-297.explanation: If patient serum was omitted, no patient antibody could bind. AHG would still remain active, allowing check cells to react and falsely reassure staff about the incomplete test.
optionExplanations: Routine overwashing is not the best explanation with positive check cells.
Prolonged centrifugation more often creates false positives.
Omitted serum explains negative screening with valid check cells.
Neutralized AHG would usually make check cells fail.
boc-1-297.memory: Check cells validate AHG, not every previous addition.

quickCheck.question: Can positive check cells prove patient serum was added?
quickCheck.answer: No; they only verify the final AHG activity.

boc-1-298.questionInPlainEnglish: How can a suspected antibody to a high-prevalence antigen be confirmed?
boc-1-298.explanation: Test rare cells known to lack candidate antigens. Nonreactivity with a target-negative cell narrows the specificity while ordinary target-positive cells continue to react.
optionExplanations: Random donors usually all carry the high-prevalence target.
Known antigen-negative rare cells provide informative comparisons.
Treating only self cells does not identify the missing target.
An eluate may be unhelpful when the antibody is an alloantibody.
boc-1-298.memory: Rare negative cells are keys to high-prevalence antibody identification.

quickCheck.question: Why are ordinary random panels often uninformative here?
quickCheck.answer: Nearly every cell carries the suspected target.

boc-1-299.questionInPlainEnglish: What targets must routine polyspecific DAT reagent recognize?
boc-1-299.explanation: Anti-IgG detects antibody coating, while anti-C3d detects complement residue. Together they cover the two major routine DAT targets.
optionExplanations: IgG plus IgA omits required complement detection.
IgG plus C3d is the standard combination.
IgM plus IgA omits both standard targets.
IgM plus C3d omits standard IgG detection.

quickCheck.question: What does monospecific reagent detect?
quickCheck.answer: One defined target, such as IgG alone or C3d alone.

boc-1-300.questionInPlainEnglish: What coating is usually detected by DAT in cold agglutinin disease?
boc-1-300.explanation: Cold IgM activates complement and may detach when warmed. Complement C3d remains attached and produces the typical DAT signal.
optionExplanations: IgM may have detached before DAT testing.
IgG is not the usual cold agglutinin DAT target.
C3d is the characteristic persistent coating.
C4a is soluble and not the routine DAT target.
boc-1-300.memory: C3d records earlier cold-antibody complement activation.

quickCheck.question: Why can a cold antibody cause a positive DAT at warm testing temperatures?
quickCheck.answer: Complement fragments can remain after the antibody detaches.

boc-1-301.questionInPlainEnglish: Which antigen disappears when both glycophorin A and B are deleted?
boc-1-301.explanation: Ena is carried on glycophorin A. A homozygous Mk deletion removes glycophorin A and B, eliminating their associated antigens.
optionExplanations: Kx is carried by a different membrane protein.
Ena disappears with loss of glycophorin A.
f is an Rh-associated antigen, not a glycophorin marker.
G is an Rh-associated antigen, not a glycophorin marker.
boc-1-301.memory: No glycophorin A means no Ena.
